ID: guide.target.gutenberg-36.ja · type: reference · SHA-256: b3bd8330e626d9b0de88c6f1fb765886fc9e7fdcae3c7a2c4af390f2e7279bbb
# The War of the Worlds — Japanese translation guide (`ja`)

**Working status:** All Japanese forms below are **provisional editorial suggestions, not approved translation decisions**. The supplied project notes establish the English work's *two-book, 17+10-chapter structure*, its front matter and its imported status; they establish **no published or human-approved Japanese translation or terminology policy**. Check existing Japanese editions and project preferences before freezing spelling, titles or voices. Source node IDs refer to the supplied structured work.

## Translation brief and register

Aim for **lucid, literary Japanese with an educated, retrospective first-person voice**, capable of moving from Edwardian-style essay and precise reportage into visceral terror. Prefer **「私」** as the narrator's consistent first-person self-reference in exposition. A restrained **だ／である** narrative register is a plausible starting point, but vary sentence rhythm, degree of formality and spoken pronouns according to situation. Do not mechanically reproduce every long English period as one sprawling Japanese sentence; preserve the **logic, suspense, repetitions and sudden perspective changes**. Avoid both excessive pseudo-Meiji archaism and casually contemporary SF jargon (`n0004`, `n0013`, `n0023`, `n0029`–`n0031`).

The narrator is *not* an omniscient hero. Distinguish **what he witnessed**, **what he was told**, **what he learned after the war**, **what he now believes**, and **what he admits remains open**. Japanese expressions such as **「らしい」「という」「後に知った」「おそらく」「断定はできない」** can preserve English hedging when warranted; avoid adding them to facts the source presents as direct observations. Conversely, do not turn speculations into plain declaratives. Keep the brother's separate itinerary in **third-person report**, rather than slipping into his first-person narration (`n0017`, `n0019`–`n0020`).

## Recommended naming conventions — all tentative

| English source form | Possible Japanese rendering | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| *The War of the Worlds* | **『宇宙戦争』** | Familiar conventional title; not a project-approved title. A word-for-word title about “worlds” would be a different editorial choice. |
| H. G. Wells | **H・G・ウェルズ** | Keep the supplied byline (`n0001`). |
| Mars / Martian(s) | **火星／火星人** | 「火星人」 is the natural recurring designation; use **「火星の生物」「火星の侵略者」** selectively for the narrator's emphasis on their nonhuman anatomy, not as a gratuitous new species distinction. |
| Ogilvy / Henderson / Stent | **オギルヴィ／ヘンダーソン／ステント** | Scientists and journalist at the first cylinder; check published transliterations and consistency (`n0004`–`n0009`). |
| Mrs. Elphinstone / Miss Elphinstone | **エルフィンストン夫人／エルフィンストン嬢** | **Not the same woman**: the wife in white vs her capable younger sister-in-law. Japanese 「夫人」「嬢」 distinguishes forms of address, but use natural referential phrasing where appropriate (`n0019`–`n0020`). |
| the narrator's wife / my brother | **妻／弟** | Neither is given a personal name. Avoid invented names, and do not collapse the brother's direct reported adventures into the narrator's actions. |
| the artilleryman | **砲兵** or **砲兵の男** | Anonymous. He is a **driver in the Horse Artillery**, not a twentieth-century automobile driver; **「騎馬砲兵隊の御者」** is an option where his duty matters (`n0014`, `n0028`). |
| the curate / the vicar | **副牧師／教区牧師** | Distinct Anglican roles; avoid translating both simply as 「神父」 by default. The curate is the narrator's unnamed companion (`n0015`–`n0016`, `n0025`). |
| Woking / Horsell Common | **ウォキング／ホーセル・コモン** | *Common* means a shared-use open heath, **not** a park or “common sense.” On first mention explain it unobtrusively as 「共同利用の荒地」 or similar (`n0005`–`n0012`). |
| Maybury / Leatherhead | **メイベリー／レザーヘッド** | Home district vs the cousins' supposed place of safety (`n0012`–`n0013`, `n0030`). |
| Weybridge / Shepperton / River Wey | **ウェイブリッジ／シェパートン／ウェイ川** | Preserve the distinction between Wey and **テムズ川** at their confluence (`n0015`). |
| Byfleet / Pyrford / Chobham / Ottershaw | **バイフリート／パーフォード／チョバム／オッターショー** | Local Surrey sites; provisional phonetic spelling, not an invitation to change them by chapter. |
| Halliford / Sheen / Mortlake | **ハリフォード／シーン／モートレイク** | Distinct waypoints of the narrator's route and imprisonment (`n0016`, `n0022`–`n0027`). |
| Putney Hill / Primrose Hill | **パトニー・ヒル／プリムローズ・ヒル** | **Do not confuse:** the artilleryman's lair is at the former; the final Martian redoubt at the latter (`n0028`–`n0029`). |
| the *Thunder Child* | **〈サンダー・チャイルド〉号** | **Ship's name**, not a child character. Prefer transliteration at first mention; the literal image 「雷の子」 could be explained only if wanted for a note (`n0020`). |

Other recurring landmarks (**the Spotted Dog**, **College Arms**, **Oriental College**, **Regent's Park**, **Hyde Park**, **Blackwater**, **Ostend**) should receive a consistent one-time style choice. E.g., **〈スポッテッド・ドッグ〉亭**, **〈カレッジ・アームズ〉**, **オリエンタル・カレッジ**, **リージェンツ・パーク**, **ハイド・パーク**, **ブラックウォーター河口**, **オーステンデ**. Avoid silently treating a tavern as a university college or converting *Oriental College* into a generic contemporary school (`n0012`–`n0015`, `n0020`). Geographic transliterations here are **suggestions for review**, not verified established Japanese exonyms.

## Technology, biology and recurrent imagery

The following is a **contextual concordance**, not an enforced one-to-one dictionary.

| Original expression | Provisional Japanese base | Usage and exceptions |
|---|---|---|
| **cylinder / projectile / shot** | **円筒／飛来体・砲弾** | The interplanetary vehicle is a hot, screw-topped *cylinder*, not initially an identified spacecraft. In artillery/astronomy narration *shot* may be **砲弾**; when its nature is not yet known use **物体／飛来体**. Retain the gradually revealed artificial nature (`n0004`–`n0007`). |
| **the Thing** (often capitalised) | **その物体／それ／あの得体の知れないもの** | Use local suspense and focalisation. A single rigid noun or premature **宇宙船** would flatten the discovery (`n0004`–`n0007`). |
| **fighting-machine** | **戦闘機械** | If silhouette/action matters, **三脚歩行機械** or **三脚の巨機**. Avoid bare **戦闘機**, which now primarily means an aircraft. The mechanism contains a living Martian (`n0013`–`n0015`, `n0023`). |
| **tripod** | **三脚式の歩行機械／三本脚の巨体** | Literal **三脚** alone can imply a static stand. Do not confuse machine legs with Martian anatomy (`n0013`, `n0023`). |
| **handling-machine** | **作業機械／多腕作業機械** | A many-limbed manipulating machine, later used to search the ruins. **操作機械** might misleadingly imply a control panel. Keep it distinct from the fighting-machine (`n0023`–`n0025`). |
| **digging-machine / flying-machine** | **掘削機械／飛行機械** | Separate specialised devices; the latter is still an **experiment** before the Martians die, not a deployed air fleet (`n0023`, `n0028`–`n0029`). |
| **Heat-Ray** | **熱線** | Capitalised named weapon: consistent **熱線**; **熱線発生装置** for its generator. The destructive beam is invisible, despite accompanying light and smoke. Do **not** introduce **レーザー** or assume a proven mirror mechanism (`n0008`–`n0009`, `n0031`). |
| **Black Smoke** | **黒い毒煙** (or recurring shorter **黒煙**) | The weapon is a **heavy lethal vapour**, deliberately released from canisters. In context 「毒性の黒い蒸気」「黒い煙」 can read more naturally than repeating a formula. **Not** ordinary smoke from burning buildings; distinguish the **黒い粉／粉末** remaining after deposition (`n0018`, `n0022`, `n0031`). |
| **red weed** | **赤い草／赤い異星植物** | No single Japanese plant category fits every appearance: when it creeps up walls **赤い蔓草**, on water **赤い植物の葉状体** may fit. First mention can retain a naming formula (e.g., **「赤い草」と呼ばれる植物**). Avoid automatically **藻** or **雑草** in contexts of giant fronds and flooding (`n0023`, `n0026`–`n0030`). |
| **red creeper** | **赤い蔓草／赤い這い植物** | **Keep the original term distinction visible** until the botanical relationship is established; the text itself describes this as a transitory growth and elsewhere uses it around trees (`n0023`, `n0027`–`n0028`). |
| **hood / cowl / head of the machine** | **頭部の覆い／覆い付きの操縦部** | It encloses a Martian operator; do not confuse the **metallic hood** with the Martian's actual fleshy head (`n0014`–`n0015`, `n0023`). |
| **carrier / cage / basket** | **収容籠／金属製の籠** | Where humans are seized, the rear carrier is a terrifying practical device, not the vehicle's main body (`n0022`, `n0024`). |
| **tentacles** | **触手** | Used for Martian bodily appendages and flexible mechanical arms; when clarity requires, say **機械の触手／金属の腕** as appropriate (`n0007`, `n0013`, `n0023`). |
| **hands** (Martian tentacle groups) | **「手」** | Professor Howes's name for the two groups of eight fine tentacles; keep quotation/technical context, not ordinary human hands (`n0023`). |
| **hoot / “Aloo!” / “Ulla, ulla…”** | **鳴き声・唸り声／「アロー！」／「ウーラ、ウーラ……」** | The sound spellings are *approximate Japanese phonetic proposals only*. Once chosen, keep their sonic identity. The last wail is eerie and repetitive, **not** a translated sentence; avoid inventing Martian linguistic meanings (`n0013`, `n0023`, `n0029`). |
| **torpedo ram / ironclad** | **水雷衝角艦／装甲艦** | Period naval terminology for *Thunder Child* and surrounding warships. Do not recast it as a contemporary destroyer or submarine (`n0020`). |
| **heliograph / hussars / sappers / Maxims** | **日光反射通信器／軽騎兵／工兵／マキシム機関銃** | Establish a compact period vocabulary and keep it intelligible in action sequences (`n0011`–`n0018`). |

The **Martian head-body, lungs, brain, sixteen tentacles, blood-injection feeding, absence of digestion, budding reproduction and lack of sleep** are presented in a retrospective quasi-scientific idiom; let the passages sound informed **without asserting that these are modern biological facts** (`n0023`). Repeated words such as **“injected,” “veins,” “recipient canal,” “bacteria,” “putrefactive,”** and **“natural selection”** call for sober precise Japanese (**注入、血管、受け入れる管、細菌、腐敗、自然選択**) rather than theatrical monster-film terms. The narrator's claim that Martians communicate by **thought without a physical medium** is **his conviction**, not a discovered universal law (`n0023`).

## Narrator, dialogue and embedded registers

- **Essayist / investigator:** articulate, exact, willing to qualify his knowledge. Keep contrasts such as microscopic life vs human empire, and the repeated shifts **“then I thought” / “we now know” / “afterwards I learned.”** For the opening's long comparison, the clauses may be broken into two or three Japanese sentences as long as the ironic symmetry survives (`n0004`, `n0010`, `n0023`, `n0031`).
- **Inner crisis:** plain, compressed cries and physical details often interrupt elaborate sentences. Avoid melodramatic embellishment. His dissociation, shame, guilt and trauma should not be rendered as a uniformly stoic or triumphalist narration (`n0010`, `n0013`–`n0014`, `n0025`, `n0028`–`n0031`).
- **Artilleryman:** slang, dropped initial *h*, *ain't*, blunt class judgments and self-satisfied rhetoric. Prefer **colloquial, clipped Japanese** (e.g. 「もう負けだ」「生き延びるんだ」), perhaps a touch of rough masculine phrasing, but **do not invent a Japanese regional dialect** or make him sound inarticulate: he can reason persuasively at length (`n0012`, `n0014`–`n0015`, `n0028`). The later irony depends on the same fluent voice coexisting with laziness.
- **Curate:** initially shocked, later increasingly compulsive, Biblical and prophetic: repetitions, cries of **woe**, references to Sodom and Gomorrah, the day of the Lord and repentance. Use **聖書調の韻律** where the source quotes scripture; verify quotations against any chosen Japanese Bible version before claiming canonical wording. The narrator's rebuke **“He is not an insurance agent”** is deliberate dry irreverence and should remain sharp (`n0016`, `n0025`).
- **Mrs. / Miss Elphinstone:** Mrs. Elphinstone is anxious and repeatedly invokes **George**; the younger woman's decisiveness is shown in action more than ornate speech. Do not automatically assign genteel, old-fashioned feminine endings such as **「〜ですわ」** to every line; distinguish their temperament and roles instead (`n0019`–`n0020`).
- **Crowds and minor speakers:** paper-sellers, soldiers and workers supply short dialect-marked utterances, newspaper headlines and rumor. Natural colloquial contrasts suffice; do not turn nineteenth-century London class and accent variation into a collection of unrelated Japanese dialect caricatures (`n0007`, `n0012`, `n0017`, `n0019`).
- **Newspapers and military reports:** headings are often sensational or misleading. Give them abrupt display formatting where appropriate, distinct from the narrator's own claims. Retain titles such as *The Times*, *Daily Telegraph*, *Daily Chronicle* and *Daily Mail* as period markers, adding Japanese glosses only where useful (`n0004`, `n0006`, `n0017`, `n0030`).

Some titles intentionally retain interpretive openness. **“Under Foot”** is both literal physical subjection and humanity's new status; **“The Work of Fifteen Days”** invokes the landscape transformed during the narrator's confinement, not merely his personal work; **“Wreckage”** spans physical damage and mental aftermath (`n0022`, `n0027`, `n0030`).

## Editorial watchpoints for Japanese continuity

1. **Retrospective science is not a corrected textbook.** Preserve period terms and limits of certainty, including the speculative parabolic Heat-Ray mirror, Martian thought exchange, possible Venus landing and alleged microbe-free Mars. In `n0029`, the narrator declares bacteria the destroyers; in `n0031` he explicitly says Carver's explanation is *not a proven conclusion*. A Japanese rendering must retain that change in epistemic status.
2. **A source-level spectral discrepancy needs a note, not a hidden correction:** **four blue spectral lines** for the unknown element in `n0018` versus **three green lines** in the black-powder analysis of `n0031`. Both are in the supplied text. Preserve both unless independent edition review establishes an authorized emendation.
3. **Do not prematurely resolve unresolved fates.** The wife ultimately lives despite a report of Leatherhead's destruction (`n0030`); the brother's life after embarkation and George Elphinstone's fate are not specified (`n0020`). The curate is struck with the **blunt** end of the chopper, then taken away, not depicted being stabbed (`n0025`). The third Martian by the naval battle is obscured (`n0020`).
4. **Historical dehumanising language should remain attributable.** The opening's **“inferior races”** is a racist nineteenth-century hierarchy introduced as part of the narrator's argument about human colonial extermination (`n0004`). A historically faithful **「劣等人種」** in context, potentially supported by an editorial note, preserves the disturbing wording more honestly than either endorsing it in neutral narration or disguising the racial hierarchy. Similarly preserve the artilleryman's harsh distinction between “fit” survivors and disposable “weaklings” as **his own speech**, not an editorial recommendation (`n0028`).
5. **Metaphors form a network.** Tiny creatures under the microscope, ants crushed by people, the dodo, a hunted rabbit, sheep, the colonised and the Martians' “eatable ants” all reverse humanity's presumed dominion (`n0004`, `n0010`, `n0018`, `n0027`–`n0028`). Preserve the exact animal chosen in each place: reusing one generic **「虫けら」** everywhere would flatten the motif.
6. **Distinguish belief, fear and irony.** The narrator's confidence in military defeat of the invaders, the curate's eschatology and the artilleryman's underground utopia are repeatedly exposed as partial or self-serving. Do not remove the narrator's bitter humour or self-implication for the sake of a unified heroic voice (`n0010`, `n0016`, `n0025`, `n0028`).
7. **Keep typography/measurement policy stable but reviewable.** Japanese dialogue can use **「　」**, interior citations **『　』**, and em dashes/ellipses as needed. Preserve meaningful headline breaks, the unfinished prophecy **“In about two hundred years …”** (`n0030`), capitalisation of named weapons through consistent terminology, and the epigraph's **Kepler — quoted in *The Anatomy of Melancholy*** attribution (`n0001`). Retain imperial distances, pounds sterling and period military designations initially; if editorial policy later adopts conversions or modernised orthography, apply it systematically rather than silently.

**Approval checkpoint:** Before chapter translation begins, confirm the published-title policy, canonical spelling of high-frequency proper names, whether **黒い毒煙** or **黒煙** is the preferred label, the strategy for **赤い草／赤い蔓草**, the two alien sound transcriptions, and Japanese narrative register. None has been approved by the supplied materials.


## Existing project context: policy.md (reference data)
# Editorial policy

## Aim

Translate or modernize as though the original author had been born a contemporary
speaker of the target language and become a novelist. This is a working editorial
question, not a claim that we can reconstruct a uniquely correct answer.

## Scope

Choose public-domain works that the maintainer expects contemporary readers to
enjoy once the linguistic distance is reduced. Selection is a matter of taste and
project scope, not a universal judgment about a book's merit or accessibility.
Do not select a work that would require turning it into a substantially different
book to achieve that aim.

Preserve the story, characters, setting, narrative viewpoint, events and larger
narrative organization. Abridgement, new scenes, reordered chapters and structural
adaptation are outside the present scope. Retain the source's meaningful
Book/Volume/Chapter divisions and their order; translate existing book titles and
headings without inventing missing ones. Publishing the whole work as a single
EPUB does not erase its internal divisions. Contemporary language does not mean
moving the story into the present day.

Sentence boundaries, paragraphing and phrasing may change freely in service of
that aim. Do not preserve an awkward sentence merely to retain correspondence.
Do not mistake completeness for sentence-by-sentence literalism.

No universal house style, target sentence length, mandatory model or prescribed
translation procedure is established here. Record work-specific decisions only
when experience shows that they are useful. A whole new translation is a normal
possible revision, not a failure of the workflow.

# Editorial policy

## Aim

Translate or modernize as though the original author had been born a contemporary
speaker of the target language and become a novelist. This is a working editorial
question, not a claim that we can reconstruct a uniquely correct answer.

## Scope

Choose public-domain works that the maintainer expects contemporary readers to
enjoy once the linguistic distance is reduced. Selection is a matter of taste and
project scope, not a universal judgment about a book's merit or accessibility.
Do not select a work that would require turning it into a substantially different
book to achieve that aim.

Preserve the story, characters, setting, narrative viewpoint, events and larger
narrative organization. Abridgement, new scenes, reordered chapters and structural
adaptation are outside the present scope. Retain the source's meaningful
Book/Volume/Chapter divisions and their order; translate existing book titles and
headings without inventing missing ones. Publishing the whole work as a single
EPUB does not erase its internal divisions. Contemporary language does not mean
moving the story into the present day.

Sentence boundaries, paragraphing and phrasing may change freely in service of
that aim. Do not preserve an awkward sentence merely to retain correspondence.
Do not mistake completeness for sentence-by-sentence literalism.

No universal house style, target sentence length, mandatory model or prescribed
translation procedure is established here. Record work-specific decisions only
when experience shows that they are useful. A whole new translation is a normal
possible revision, not a failure of the workflow.


## Material 2: The War of the Worlds — work reference (language-neutral)
ID: guide.work.gutenberg-36 · type: reference · SHA-256: 62c909253fcad3b07d3fa390b95aff0503b348f72e6ae9e48e92bb4fccaf34c7
# The War of the Worlds — work reference (language-neutral)

**Source:** H. G. Wells, Project Gutenberg work `gutenberg-36` (English). **Scope:** the supplied structured literary text, from the title, byline and Kepler epigraph (`n0001`) through both books and the epilogue (`n0031`), including the contents (`n0002`). **Status:** this is an AI-produced reference, not an approved interpretation or a human review. The supplied source notes describe the acquisition as *imported*, not *reviewed*, and do not establish the precise historical print exemplar. It should be used with the source, not as a replacement for reading it.

## Structure, narrative perspective and time

- **Two books, not two separate works.** Book One, **“The Coming of the Martians”** (`n0003`), has 17 chapters (`n0004`–`n0020`); Book Two, **“The Earth Under the Martians”** (`n0021`), has 10 (`n0022`–`n0031`). Chapter numbers restart in Book Two. The contents reproduce the chapter headings but are separate front matter. Preserve the supplied actual body headings and their punctuation as the structural source of truth; the Kepler quotation and its attribution belong before the contents (`n0001`–`n0002`).
- The main **first-person narrator is unnamed**. He lives with his unnamed wife at Maybury, near Woking, and writes speculative/philosophical essays. He recounts events **after** the invasion with hindsight, later research, reconstructed reports, direct address to the reader and pointed admissions of uncertainty. His narrative is not a continuous real-time diary. He sometimes steps back into an almost omniscient account, then qualifies what he could know (`n0004`, `n0011`, `n0018`, `n0030`–`n0031`).
- The narrative explicitly leaves his perspective to follow his **younger brother in London and on the eastward evacuation** (`n0017`, `n0019`–`n0020`). The switch is purposeful and marked by phrases such as “my brother”; these scenes must not be converted into experiences personally witnessed by the narrator. Book Two opens by returning to the narrator and the curate's confinement (`n0022`).
- The arrival happens in **June**, on a **Friday** (`n0005`–`n0011`, `n0020`, `n0024`). Observed Martian activity in 1894 precedes the attack; the narrator says the catastrophe was **six years ago** from his later vantage and situates the shock in the early twentieth century (`n0004`). These signals do not license inserting a precise calendar date. Ten discharges from Mars are reported, but the text does not give a complete individual landing narrative for all ten (`n0004`, `n0028`).

## Characters, identities and relationships

| Figure | Stable reference and narrative function |
|---|---|
| **The unnamed narrator** | Educated writer of speculative philosophy, initially complacent and fascinated by the military response; alternates curiosity, panic, detached observation, cruelty, self-justification and sympathy. His abandoned treatise about the future of moral ideas becomes pointedly ironic on his return (`n0004`, `n0010`, `n0025`, `n0028`, `n0030`). |
| **His unnamed wife** | Sent by him to **her cousins at Leatherhead** during the early fighting (`n0012`–`n0013`); the narrator spends most of the book trying to return to her. Her survival and return to Woking are revealed unexpectedly at the end, despite later reports that Leatherhead was destroyed (`n0030`–`n0031`). Do not supply a name or invent the details of her escape. |
| **His unnamed younger brother** | Medical student in London; supplies the London panic and Essex-coast escape strand, not eyewitness information from Woking. He saves and travels with the Elphinstone women and boards a vessel bound for Ostend (`n0017`, `n0019`–`n0020`). The text does not narrate his subsequent life or a reunion with the narrator. |
| **Mrs. Elphinstone** | Surgeon George's wife, **the woman in white**; frightened, repeatedly wishes to return to Stanmore and find her husband. Distinct from **Miss Elphinstone**, her husband's younger sister (`n0019`–`n0020`). |
| **Miss Elphinstone** | The **younger, dark, slender sister-in-law**: capable, calm under stress, uses the revolver, helps the brother in danger and advocates escape by sea. Do not confuse her role or family position with Mrs. Elphinstone (`n0019`–`n0020`). |
| **George** | The Elphinstone women's absent surgeon relative: Mrs. Elphinstone's husband and Miss Elphinstone's brother. His promised reunion with them is not shown (`n0019`–`n0020`). |
| **Ogilvy** | Astronomer and acquaintance of the narrator; observes Mars, first investigates the cylinder and tries to assist the presumed occupants. Killed as a member of the white-flag deputation (`n0004`–`n0009`). |
| **Henderson** | London journalist who examines the cylinder with Ogilvy and attempts to telegraph the news; killed in the deputation (`n0005`, `n0008`–`n0011`). |
| **Stent** | Identified in this source as the **Astronomer Royal**; oversees excavation/precautions and is killed with the deputation (`n0006`–`n0009`). **Lord Hilton** is the local lord of the manor whom the narrator is sent to seek, not a participant in that deputation (`n0006`). |
| **The artilleryman** | Unnamed driver of No. 12 Horse Artillery, rescued from battle; initially shares the narrator's house and flight, then reappears near Putney Hill (`n0014`–`n0015`, `n0028`). His elaborate survivalist plan and selective vision are undermined by his negligible digging and fondness for food, drink and games. His eloquence should not be taken as the author's settled prescription. |
| **The curate** | Unnamed Anglican assistant clergyman encountered after Weybridge; initially interprets disaster as divine judgment, then mentally unravels during captivity. The narrator strikes him with the **back/blunt end** of a meat chopper to silence him; the handling-machine subsequently takes his body. The text treats him as dead but does not show the actual instant of death (`n0016`, `n0022`–`n0026`, `n0028`). Keep both the narrator's responsibility and the limits of his observation. |
| **Secondary named observers and authorities** | **Schiaparelli, Perrotin, Lavelle, Albin, Denning** connect astronomical testimony; **Markham** is a newspaper editor (`n0004`–`n0005`). **Professor Howes** names Martian tentacle groups “hands”; **Philips** comments on Martian colour vision (`n0023`). **Carver** advances the disease hypothesis and **Lessing** the possible Venus landing (`n0031`). None is a hidden alias of the narrator. |

## Geographical continuity

**Arrival and Surrey fighting:** The first cylinder lands at the sandpits of **Horsell Common** near **Woking**; the narrator's house is at **Maybury**. Nearby **Ottershaw, Chobham, Byfleet, Pyrford, Addlestone, Weybridge, Shepperton, Chertsey** and the Rivers **Wey** and **Thames** matter to the advance, artillery lines and river escape (`n0005`–`n0018`). **Leatherhead** is initially imagined as safety for the narrator's wife but is later reported destroyed (`n0012`, `n0030`). The destroyed *Oriental College*, its mosque, the *Spotted Dog* inn, and the *College Arms* are named local landmarks, not generic settings (`n0012`–`n0015`).

**Narrator's Thames/London route:** After Weybridge he drifts downstream towards **Walton/Halliford** and joins the curate; they move through **Sunbury, Hampton Court, Twickenham, Richmond, Kew and Sheen**, where the **fifth cylinder** buries them beside its pit. After the confinement, he moves through **Mortlake, Roehampton and Putney**, reunites with the artilleryman near **Putney Hill**, then travels through **Fulham, South Kensington, Hyde Park, Regent's Park** and **Primrose Hill**, the site of the Martians' major London redoubt (`n0016`, `n0022`–`n0029`). He ultimately returns by railway via **Byfleet** to Woking (`n0030`). The narrative's shifting riversides and bridges are significant; do not flatten them to “around London.”

**Brother's separate route:** From London around **Regent's Park**, he attempts to flee via **Chalk Farm, Edgware and Barnet**, joins Mrs. and Miss Elphinstone, and heads through **Essex**, **Chelmsford** and **Tillingham** to the **Blackwater estuary/Essex coast**. Their crowded **paddle steamer** is bound for **Ostend**, witnessed during the naval engagement with *Thunder Child* (`n0017`, `n0019`–`n0020`). Distinguish **Putney Hill** from **Primrose Hill**, and the ordinary **common lands** from parks and streets.

## Event and causal anchors (not a complete synopsis)

1. **Before arrival:** Martian flashes observed telescopically; ten nearly daily launches go unrecognised as weapons. The first hot, screw-topped cylinder is misidentified as a meteorite; curious spectators expect humanoids (`n0004`–`n0007`).
2. **Friday–Saturday:** Ogilvy, Stent, Henderson and others approach with a white flag; the **Heat-Ray** annihilates them. News remains fragmentary. The military responds; Woking is devastated; the narrator sends his wife to Leatherhead and returns to find **giant walking fighting-machines** (`n0008`–`n0014`). The second cylinder arrives just after Friday midnight and the third during the narrator's Saturday-night storm (`n0011`, `n0013`).
3. **Sunday:** In the Weybridge–Shepperton battle, concealed guns kill **one Martian inside its fighting-machine**; the stricken machine crashes into the river. The other machines withdraw, carrying away its wreckage. The narrator meets the curate; his brother observes London's slow awakening (`n0015`–`n0017`).
4. **Sunday night–Monday:** The invaders fire canisters of **Black Smoke**, a heavy lethal vapour that follows low ground, and render organised defences ineffective. The fourth cylinder falls in Bushey Park; panic empties London. The narrator and curate become trapped when the fifth cylinder destroys most of a house near Sheen; the sixth lands at Wimbledon (`n0018`–`n0022`).
5. **Coastal escape:** The brother and Elphinstone women reach a steamer off Essex. The torpedo ram **_Thunder Child_** defeats **two Martian machines**, the second in its own fiery collision; the view of the ship and **third Martian** is then lost in steam and smoke. Their definitive fates are not observed in that scene (`n0020`). The artilleryman's later assertion that the Martians have lost only one reflects **his limited knowledge**, not a corrected casualty total (`n0028`).
6. **Confinement and reversal:** During about **fifteen days** in the buried kitchen/scullery, the narrator sees Martian industry and feeding, quarrels with the curate, strikes him, and narrowly escapes a probing mechanical tentacle. On emerging he finds an alien-looking landscape overrun with **red weed**; the weed begins to decline from a presumed terrestrial disease (`n0023`–`n0027`).
7. **Last phase and aftermath:** The artilleryman's underground civilisation is revealed to be more oratory than labour. The narrator finds stationary Martians in London and reaches the **Primrose Hill** redoubt: they are dead, attributed to Earth microorganisms. In later reflection the explanation is called **strongly probable, not conclusively proved**. He undergoes a period of mental disturbance, is told Leatherhead was destroyed, returns to his house and unexpectedly reunites with his wife. The epilogue leaves future invasion and a possible Venus landing open (`n0028`–`n0031`).

## Recurring systems and concrete distinctions

- **Martians themselves:** Not humanoids. Mature creatures have enormous head-bodies (about four feet across), large eyes, beak-like mouth, sixteen fine tentacles in two groups, lungs and central nervous structures; weak terrestrial mobility; no digestive system as humans understand it. They take **fresh blood from living prey**, including humans, directly into their own circulation. Reproduction by **budding**, absence of sex and sleep, and purported freedom from disease are presented in the narrator's scientific retrospective (`n0007`, `n0023`–`n0024`). Mars-based bipedal **food animals** found in cylinders are **not Martians** (`n0023`).
- **Different machines:** The towering three-legged **fighting-machine** carries the operator, Heat-Ray and sometimes a carrier for captives (`n0013`–`n0015`, `n0022`). The agile, many-armed **handling-machine** works on materials and can probe the house (`n0023`–`n0025`). Also distinguish a digging/excavating mechanism, material-processing equipment that makes aluminium from clay, and an experimental **flying-machine** at Primrose Hill (`n0023`–`n0024`, `n0028`–`n0029`). The narrator stresses their supple, nearly organic articulation and the **absence of wheels**, contrary to anachronistic mechanical imagery (`n0023`).
- **Heat-Ray:** An effectively invisible directed beam of destructive heat; solid materials burn/melt and struck water erupts as steam. A parabolic-mirror account is **a theory, not verified mechanism**. Green smoke, light and sparks seen around equipment are not themselves the same as the invisible beam (`n0008`–`n0009`, `n0031`).
- **Black Smoke:** Not ordinary fire smoke. A canister releases a dense poisonous vapour that accumulates in hollows, can leave upper storeys relatively safer, reacts with water and eventually settles as **black dust/powder**. Martians also disperse it by **steam jets**. Its chemical composition remains unsettled (`n0018`, `n0022`, `n0031`). Do not confuse the poisoning with heat damage or the dark soot of conventional fires.
- **Red weed / red creeper:** Extraterrestrial growth spreads spectacularly after the Martian landing, particularly through **flowing water**, clogs rivers and causes flooding, then decays, apparently under the influence of local bacteria (`n0023`, `n0026`–`n0030`). The text also names a **“red creeper,”** once described as shorter-lived; do not silently assume that every reference denotes the same plant or that all colour terms refer to one botanical structure (`n0023`, `n0027`–`n0028`).
- **Sounds:** The metallic machines produce hoots and **“Aloo! Aloo!”** (`n0013`); a late stationary Martian emits the unending, mournful **“Ulla, ulla…”** (`n0029`). The narrator's retrospective **telepathy hypothesis** contests others' assumption that hooting is Martian conversation; he claims the hoot precedes feeding, but it remains an inference (`n0023`). Do not interpret the sound strings as confirmed words or translate them into invented dialogue.
- **Nineteenth-century context:** Heliographs, telegraph wires, special newspaper editions, horse artillery, hussars, Maxim guns, steam railways, horse-drawn cabs, bicycles, early motor cars and naval ironclads coexist. The **torpedo ram _Thunder Child_** is a distinct historical-style *type of warship*, not a modern missile boat or aircraft (`n0011`–`n0020`).

## Voice, motifs and ethical tensions

The texture alternates **measured speculative-scientific exposition**, precise topographical reportage and quoted dispatches, vivid physical terror, socially distinctive dialogue and abrupt psychological confession. The narrator can describe whole populations with the cool eye of a naturalist and then break into personal panic. He repeatedly addresses a reader presumed to live after the catastrophe (`n0004`, `n0009`, `n0011`, `n0020`, `n0031`). Preserve the switches instead of smoothing everything into heroic action prose.

A central reversal is **humanity becoming the animal or colonised subject**: microscopy, insects, ants, rabbits, dogs, the extinct dodo and dispossession recur. The opening invokes the destruction inflicted by European colonists on Indigenous Tasmanians and uses a nineteenth-century hierarchy of “inferior races” (`n0004`); the narrator later learns pity for the creatures humanity dominates (`n0027`–`n0028`). These passages are uncomfortable historically situated language, not terminology to endorse or unobtrusively sanitise. Class prejudice, military bravado, unreliable sensational journalism, religious collapse/repentance, survivalist eugenic fantasies and the narrator's own violence invite critical distance (`n0012`, `n0016`–`n0019`, `n0024`–`n0028`).

The catastrophe does **not** end in a straightforward military victory. Powerful human weapons occasionally wound or destroy machines, but the decisive reversal is attributed to microbes. The narrator's delight at recovery coexists with dislocation and recurring traumatic visions; his future remains insecure even with his wife alive (`n0029`–`n0031`). The epilogue imagines both a **human cosmic future** and renewed subjection. Keep the final balance unresolved.

## Ambiguities and open research questions

- **Disease explanation:** The main narration presents bacterial defeat as definite (`n0029`), but the epilogue acknowledges **Carver's hypothesis remains unproved** (`n0031`). Mark the difference between assertive storytelling and formal epistemic status; do not silently eliminate it.
- **Spectral particulars:** The early Black Smoke account refers to an unknown element yielding **four lines in the blue** (`n0018`), while the epilogue's analysis of its **black powder residue** says **three lines in the green** (`n0031`). They may concern different material states/observations, or be a source inconsistency; preserve the text and flag for later edition checking rather than harmonising it.
- **Martian communication:** Sound vs telepathy remains narrator-inferred; **Venus colonisation** is Lessing's suggestion, not a confirmed sequel; the circumstances and aims behind the cessation of the ten shots remain unknown (`n0004`, `n0023`, `n0031`).
- **Unseen fates:** The wife's escape from Leatherhead, the brother's later movements after leaving by sea, George Elphinstone's fate, and the naval encounter's obscured third Martian are not supplied in full (`n0020`, `n0030`). Maintain narrative gaps.
- **Human culpability:** The curate's actual moment of death occurs outside view and the narrator evaluates his own blow defensively; the artilleryman's harsh programme is undercut by his behaviour, not confirmed as a feasible salvation (`n0025`, `n0028`). Avoid certainties of motive or culpability beyond the words on the page.
- **Textual provenance:** Source notes cite an 1898 Heinemann first-edition record but **do not demonstrate that the Gutenberg transcription is copied from that edition**. The imported structural segmentation has not received independent human review. For contested spelling, punctuation, scientific discrepancies and attribution, compare an authenticated exemplar before making editorial corrections.


## Material 3: The War of the Worlds — Japanese translation guide (`ja`)
ID: guide.target.gutenberg-36.ja · type: reference · SHA-256: b3bd8330e626d9b0de88c6f1fb765886fc9e7fdcae3c7a2c4af390f2e7279bbb
# The War of the Worlds — Japanese translation guide (`ja`)

**Working status:** All Japanese forms below are **provisional editorial suggestions, not approved translation decisions**. The supplied project notes establish the English work's *two-book, 17+10-chapter structure*, its front matter and its imported status; they establish **no published or human-approved Japanese translation or terminology policy**. Check existing Japanese editions and project preferences before freezing spelling, titles or voices. Source node IDs refer to the supplied structured work.

## Translation brief and register

Aim for **lucid, literary Japanese with an educated, retrospective first-person voice**, capable of moving from Edwardian-style essay and precise reportage into visceral terror. Prefer **「私」** as the narrator's consistent first-person self-reference in exposition. A restrained **だ／である** narrative register is a plausible starting point, but vary sentence rhythm, degree of formality and spoken pronouns according to situation. Do not mechanically reproduce every long English period as one sprawling Japanese sentence; preserve the **logic, suspense, repetitions and sudden perspective changes**. Avoid both excessive pseudo-Meiji archaism and casually contemporary SF jargon (`n0004`, `n0013`, `n0023`, `n0029`–`n0031`).

The narrator is *not* an omniscient hero. Distinguish **what he witnessed**, **what he was told**, **what he learned after the war**, **what he now believes**, and **what he admits remains open**. Japanese expressions such as **「らしい」「という」「後に知った」「おそらく」「断定はできない」** can preserve English hedging when warranted; avoid adding them to facts the source presents as direct observations. Conversely, do not turn speculations into plain declaratives. Keep the brother's separate itinerary in **third-person report**, rather than slipping into his first-person narration (`n0017`, `n0019`–`n0020`).

## Recommended naming conventions — all tentative

| English source form | Possible Japanese rendering | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| *The War of the Worlds* | **『宇宙戦争』** | Familiar conventional title; not a project-approved title. A word-for-word title about “worlds” would be a different editorial choice. |
| H. G. Wells | **H・G・ウェルズ** | Keep the supplied byline (`n0001`). |
| Mars / Martian(s) | **火星／火星人** | 「火星人」 is the natural recurring designation; use **「火星の生物」「火星の侵略者」** selectively for the narrator's emphasis on their nonhuman anatomy, not as a gratuitous new species distinction. |
| Ogilvy / Henderson / Stent | **オギルヴィ／ヘンダーソン／ステント** | Scientists and journalist at the first cylinder; check published transliterations and consistency (`n0004`–`n0009`). |
| Mrs. Elphinstone / Miss Elphinstone | **エルフィンストン夫人／エルフィンストン嬢** | **Not the same woman**: the wife in white vs her capable younger sister-in-law. Japanese 「夫人」「嬢」 distinguishes forms of address, but use natural referential phrasing where appropriate (`n0019`–`n0020`). |
| the narrator's wife / my brother | **妻／弟** | Neither is given a personal name. Avoid invented names, and do not collapse the brother's direct reported adventures into the narrator's actions. |
| the artilleryman | **砲兵** or **砲兵の男** | Anonymous. He is a **driver in the Horse Artillery**, not a twentieth-century automobile driver; **「騎馬砲兵隊の御者」** is an option where his duty matters (`n0014`, `n0028`). |
| the curate / the vicar | **副牧師／教区牧師** | Distinct Anglican roles; avoid translating both simply as 「神父」 by default. The curate is the narrator's unnamed companion (`n0015`–`n0016`, `n0025`). |
| Woking / Horsell Common | **ウォキング／ホーセル・コモン** | *Common* means a shared-use open heath, **not** a park or “common sense.” On first mention explain it unobtrusively as 「共同利用の荒地」 or similar (`n0005`–`n0012`). |
| Maybury / Leatherhead | **メイベリー／レザーヘッド** | Home district vs the cousins' supposed place of safety (`n0012`–`n0013`, `n0030`). |
| Weybridge / Shepperton / River Wey | **ウェイブリッジ／シェパートン／ウェイ川** | Preserve the distinction between Wey and **テムズ川** at their confluence (`n0015`). |

E.g., **〈スポッテッド・ドッグ〉亭**, **〈カレッジ・アームズ〉**, **オリエンタル・カレッジ**, **リージェンツ・パーク**, **ハイド・パーク**, **ブラックウォーター河口**, **オーステンデ**. Avoid silently treating a tavern as a university college or converting *Oriental College* into a generic contemporary school (`n0012`–`n0015`, `n0020`). Geographic transliterations here are **suggestions for review**, not verified established Japanese exonyms.

The following is a **contextual concordance**, not an enforced one-to-one dictionary.

| **Black Smoke** | **黒い毒煙** (or recurring shorter **黒煙**) | The weapon is a **heavy lethal vapour**, deliberately released from canisters. In context 「毒性の黒い蒸気」「黒い煙」 can read more naturally than repeating a formula. **Not** ordinary smoke from burning buildings; distinguish the **黒い粉／粉末** remaining after deposition (`n0018`, `n0022`, `n0031`). |

First mention can retain a naming formula (e.g., **「赤い草」と呼ばれる植物**). Avoid automatically **藻** or **雑草** in contexts of giant fronds and flooding (`n0023`, `n0026`–`n0030`). |
| **red creeper** | **赤い蔓草／赤い這い植物** | **Keep the original term distinction visible** until the botanical relationship is established; the text itself describes this as a transitory growth and elsewhere uses it around trees (`n0023`, `n0027`–`n0028`). |
| **hood / cowl / head of the machine** | **頭部の覆い／覆い付きの操縦部** | It encloses a Martian operator; do not confuse the **metallic hood** with the Martian's actual fleshy head (`n0014`–`n0015`, `n0023`). |
| **carrier / cage / basket** | **収容籠／金属製の籠** | Where humans are seized, the rear carrier is a terrifying practical device, not the vehicle's main body (`n0022`, `n0024`). |

| **hands** (Martian tentacle groups) | **「手」** | Professor Howes's name for the two groups of eight fine tentacles; keep quotation/technical context, not ordinary human hands (`n0023`). |
| **hoot / “Aloo!” / “Ulla, ulla…”** | **鳴き声・唸り声／「アロー！」／「ウーラ、ウーラ……」** | The sound spellings are *approximate Japanese phonetic proposals only*. Once chosen, keep their sonic identity. The **Martian head-body, lungs, brain, sixteen tentacles, blood-injection feeding, absence of digestion, budding reproduction and lack of sleep** are presented in a retrospective quasi-scientific idiom; let the passages sound informed **without asserting that these are modern biological facts** (`n0023`). Repeated words such as **“injected,” “veins,” “recipient canal,” “bacteria,” “putrefactive,”** and **“natural selection”** call for sober precise Japanese (**注入、血管、受け入れる管、細菌、腐敗、自然選択**) rather than theatrical monster-film terms. The narrator's claim that Martians communicate by **thought without a physical medium** is **his conviction**, not a discovered universal law (`n0023`).

- **Essayist / investigator:** articulate, exact, willing to qualify his knowledge. Keep contrasts such as microscopic life vs human empire, and the repeated shifts **“then I thought” / “we now know” / “afterwards I learned.”** For the opening's long comparison, the clauses may be broken into two or three Japanese sentences as long as the ironic symmetry survives (`n0004`, `n0010`, `n0023`, `n0031`).
- **Inner crisis:** plain, compressed cries and physical details often interrupt elaborate sentences. Avoid melodramatic embellishment. His dissociation, shame, guilt and trauma should not be rendered as a uniformly stoic or triumphalist narration (`n0010`, `n0013`–`n0014`, `n0025`, `n0028`–`n0031`).
- **Artilleryman:** slang, dropped initial *h*, *ain't*, blunt class judgments and self-satisfied rhetoric. Prefer **colloquial, clipped Japanese** (e.g. 「もう負けだ」「生き延びるんだ」), perhaps a touch of rough masculine phrasing, but **do not invent a Japanese regional dialect** or make him sound inarticulate: he can reason persuasively at length (`n0012`, `n0014`–`n0015`, `n0028`). The later irony depends on the same fluent voice coexisting with laziness.
- **Curate:** initially shocked, later increasingly compulsive, Biblical and prophetic: repetitions, cries of **woe**, references to Sodom and Gomorrah, the day of the Lord and repentance. Use **聖書調の韻律** where the source quotes scripture; verify quotations against any chosen Japanese Bible version before claiming canonical wording. The narrator's rebuke **“He is not an insurance agent”** is deliberate dry irreverence and should remain sharp (`n0016`, `n0025`).
- **Mrs. / Miss Elphinstone:** Mrs. Elphinstone is anxious and repeatedly invokes **George**; the younger woman's decisiveness is shown in action more than ornate speech. Do not automatically assign genteel, old-fashioned feminine endings such as **「〜ですわ」** to every line; distinguish their temperament and roles instead (`n0019`–`n0020`).
- **Crowds and minor speakers:** paper-sellers, soldiers and workers supply short dialect-marked utterances, newspaper headlines and rumor. Natural colloquial contrasts suffice; do not turn nineteenth-century London class and accent variation into a collection of unrelated Japanese dialect caricatures (`n0007`, `n0012`, `n0017`, `n0019`).
- **Newspapers and military reports:** headings are often sensational or misleading. Give them abrupt display formatting where appropriate, distinct from the narrator's own claims. ## Editorial watchpoints for Japanese continuity

1. **Retrospective science is not a corrected textbook.** Preserve period terms and limits of certainty, including the speculative parabolic Heat-Ray mirror, Martian thought exchange, possible Venus landing and alleged microbe-free Mars. In `n0029`, the narrator declares bacteria the destroyers; in `n0031` he explicitly says Carver's explanation is *not a proven conclusion*. A Japanese rendering must retain that change in epistemic status.
2. **A source-level spectral discrepancy needs a note, not a hidden correction:** **four blue spectral lines** for the unknown element in `n0018` versus **three green lines** in the black-powder analysis of `n0031`. Both are in the supplied text. Preserve both unless independent edition review establishes an authorized emendation.
3. **Do not prematurely resolve unresolved fates.** The wife ultimately lives despite a report of Leatherhead's destruction (`n0030`); the brother's life after embarkation and George Elphinstone's fate are not specified (`n0020`). The curate is struck with the **blunt** end of the chopper, then taken away, not depicted being stabbed (`n0025`). The third Martian by the naval battle is obscured (`n0020`).
4. **Historical dehumanising language should remain attributable.** The opening's **“inferior races”** is a racist nineteenth-century hierarchy introduced as part of the narrator's argument about human colonial extermination (`n0004`). A historically faithful **「劣等人種」** in context, potentially supported by an editorial note, preserves the disturbing wording more honestly than either endorsing it in neutral narration or disguising the racial hierarchy. Similarly preserve the artilleryman's harsh distinction between “fit” survivors and disposable “weaklings” as **his own speech**, not an editorial recommendation (`n0028`).
5. **Metaphors form a network.** Tiny creatures under the microscope, ants crushed by people, the dodo, a hunted rabbit, sheep, the colonised and the Martians' “eatable ants” all reverse humanity's presumed dominion (`n0004`, `n0010`, `n0018`, `n0027`–`n0028`). Preserve the exact animal chosen in each place: reusing one generic **「虫けら」** everywhere would flatten the motif.
6. **Distinguish belief, fear and irony.** The narrator's confidence in military defeat of the invaders, the curate's eschatology and the artilleryman's underground utopia are repeatedly exposed as partial or self-serving. Do not remove the narrator's bitter humour or self-implication for the sake of a unified heroic voice (`n0010`, `n0016`, `n0025`, `n0028`).
7. **Keep typography/measurement policy stable but reviewable.** Japanese dialogue can use **「　」**, interior citations **『　』**, and em dashes/ellipses as needed. Preserve meaningful headline breaks, the unfinished prophecy **“In about two hundred years …”** (`n0030`), capitalisation of named weapons through consistent terminology, and the epigraph's **Kepler — quoted in *The Anatomy of Melancholy*** attribution (`n0001`). Retain imperial distances, pounds sterling and period military designations initially; if editorial policy later adopts conversions or modernised orthography, apply it systematically rather than silently.

# Editorial policy

## Aim

Translate or modernize as though the original author had been born a contemporary
speaker of the target language and become a novelist. This is a working editorial
question, not a claim that we can reconstruct a uniquely correct answer.

## Scope

Choose public-domain works that the maintainer expects contemporary readers to
enjoy once the linguistic distance is reduced. Selection is a matter of taste and
project scope, not a universal judgment about a book's merit or accessibility.
Do not select a work that would require turning it into a substantially different
book to achieve that aim.

Preserve the story, characters, setting, narrative viewpoint, events and larger
narrative organization. Abridgement, new scenes, reordered chapters and structural
adaptation are outside the present scope. Retain the source's meaningful
Book/Volume/Chapter divisions and their order; translate existing book titles and
headings without inventing missing ones. Publishing the whole work as a single
EPUB does not erase its internal divisions. Contemporary language does not mean
moving the story into the present day.

Sentence boundaries, paragraphing and phrasing may change freely in service of
that aim. Do not preserve an awkward sentence merely to retain correspondence.
Do not mistake completeness for sentence-by-sentence literalism.

No universal house style, target sentence length, mandatory model or prescribed
translation procedure is established here. Record work-specific decisions only
when experience shows that they are useful. A whole new translation is a normal
possible revision, not a failure of the workflow.

The supplied source notes describe the acquisition as *imported*, not *reviewed*, and do not establish the precise historical print exemplar. It should be used with the source, not as a replacement for reading it.

## Structure, narrative perspective and time

- **Two books, not two separate works.** Book One, **“The Coming of the Martians”** (`n0003`), has 17 chapters (`n0004`–`n0020`); Book Two, **“The Earth Under the Martians”** (`n0021`), has 10 (`n0022`–`n0031`). Chapter numbers restart in Book Two. The contents reproduce the chapter headings but are separate front matter. Preserve the supplied actual body headings and their punctuation as the structural source of truth; the Kepler quotation and its attribution belong before the contents (`n0001`–`n0002`).
- The main **first-person narrator is unnamed**. He lives with his unnamed wife at Maybury, near Woking, and writes speculative/philosophical essays. He recounts events **after** the invasion with hindsight, later research, reconstructed reports, direct address to the reader and pointed admissions of uncertainty. His narrative is not a continuous real-time diary. He sometimes steps back into an almost omniscient account, then qualifies what he could know (`n0004`, `n0011`, `n0018`, `n0030`–`n0031`).
- The narrative explicitly leaves his perspective to follow his **younger brother in London and on the eastward evacuation** (`n0017`, `n0019`–`n0020`). The switch is purposeful and marked by phrases such as “my brother”; these scenes must not be converted into experiences personally witnessed by the narrator. Book Two opens by returning to the narrator and the curate's confinement (`n0022`).
- The arrival happens in **June**, on a **Friday** (`n0005`–`n0011`, `n0020`, `n0024`). Observed Martian activity in 1894 precedes the attack; the narrator says the catastrophe was **six years ago** from his later vantage and situates the shock in the early twentieth century (`n0004`). These signals do not license inserting a precise calendar date. Ten discharges from Mars are reported, but the text does not give a complete individual landing narrative for all ten (`n0004`, `n0028`).

## Characters, identities and relationships

| Figure | Stable reference and narrative function |

| **The unnamed narrator** | Educated writer of speculative philosophy, initially complacent and fascinated by the military response; alternates curiosity, panic, detached observation, cruelty, self-justification and sympathy. His abandoned treatise about the future of moral ideas becomes pointedly ironic on his return (`n0004`, `n0010`, `n0025`, `n0028`, `n0030`). |
| **His unnamed wife** | Sent by him to **her cousins at Leatherhead** during the early fighting (`n0012`–`n0013`); the narrator spends most of the book trying to return to her. Her survival and return to Woking are revealed unexpectedly at the end, despite later reports that Leatherhead was destroyed (`n0030`–`n0031`). Do not supply a name or invent the details of her escape. |
| **His unnamed younger brother** | Medical student in London; supplies the London panic and Essex-coast escape strand, not eyewitness information from Woking. He saves and travels with the Elphinstone women and boards a vessel bound for Ostend (`n0017`, `n0019`–`n0020`). The text does not narrate his subsequent life or a reunion with the narrator. |
| **Mrs. Elphinstone** | Surgeon George's wife, **the woman in white**; frightened, repeatedly wishes to return to Stanmore and find her husband. Distinct from **Miss Elphinstone**, her husband's younger sister (`n0019`–`n0020`). |
| **Miss Elphinstone** | The **younger, dark, slender sister-in-law**: capable, calm under stress, uses the revolver, helps the brother in danger and advocates escape by sea. Do not confuse her role or family position with Mrs. Elphinstone (`n0019`–`n0020`). |

## Geographical continuity

**Arrival and Surrey fighting:** The first cylinder lands at the sandpits of **Horsell Common** near **Woking**; the narrator's house is at **Maybury**. Nearby **Ottershaw, Chobham, Byfleet, Pyrford, Addlestone, Weybridge, Shepperton, Chertsey** and the Rivers **Wey** and **Thames** matter to the advance, artillery lines and river escape (`n0005`–`n0018`). **Leatherhead** is initially imagined as safety for the narrator's wife but is later reported destroyed (`n0012`, `n0030`). The destroyed *Oriental College*, its mosque, the *Spotted Dog* inn, and the *College Arms* are named local landmarks, not generic settings (`n0012`–`n0015`).

**Narrator's Thames/London route:** After Weybridge he drifts downstream towards **Walton/Halliford** and joins the curate; they move through **Sunbury, Hampton Court, Twickenham, Richmond, Kew and Sheen**, where the **fifth cylinder** buries them beside its pit. After the confinement, he moves through **Mortlake, Roehampton and Putney**, reunites with the artilleryman near **Putney Hill**, then travels through **Fulham, South Kensington, Hyde Park, Regent's Park** and **Primrose Hill**, the site of the Martians' major London redoubt (`n0016`, `n0022`–`n0029`). He ultimately returns by railway via **Byfleet** to Woking (`n0030`). The narrative's shifting riversides and bridges are significant; do not flatten them to “around London.”

**Brother's separate route:** From London around **Regent's Park**, he attempts to flee via **Chalk Farm, Edgware and Barnet**, joins Mrs. and Miss Elphinstone, and heads through **Essex**, **Chelmsford** and **Tillingham** to the **Blackwater estuary/Essex coast**. Their crowded **paddle steamer** is bound for **Ostend**, witnessed during the naval engagement with *Thunder Child* (`n0017`, `n0019`–`n0020`). Distinguish **Putney Hill** from **Primrose Hill**, and the ordinary **common lands** from parks and streets.

## Event and causal anchors (not a complete synopsis)

1. **Before arrival:** Martian flashes observed telescopically; ten nearly daily launches go unrecognised as weapons. The first hot, screw-topped cylinder is misidentified as a meteorite; curious spectators expect humanoids (`n0004`–`n0007`).
2. **Friday–Saturday:** Ogilvy, Stent, Henderson and others approach with a white flag; the **Heat-Ray** annihilates them. News remains fragmentary. The military responds; Woking is devastated; the narrator sends his wife to Leatherhead and returns to find **giant walking fighting-machines** (`n0008`–`n0014`). The second cylinder arrives just after Friday midnight and the third during the narrator's Saturday-night storm (`n0011`, `n0013`).
3. **Sunday:** In the Weybridge–Shepperton battle, concealed guns kill **one Martian inside its fighting-machine**; the stricken machine crashes into the river. The other machines withdraw, carrying away its wreckage. The narrator meets the curate; his brother observes London's slow awakening (`n0015`–`n0017`).
4. **Sunday night–Monday:** The invaders fire canisters of **Black Smoke**, a heavy lethal vapour that follows low ground, and render organised defences ineffective. The fourth cylinder falls in Bushey Park; panic empties London. The narrator and curate become trapped when the fifth cylinder destroys most of a house near Sheen; the sixth lands at Wimbledon (`n0018`–`n0022`).
5. **Coastal escape:** The brother and Elphinstone women reach a steamer off Essex. The torpedo ram **_Thunder Child_** defeats **two Martian machines**, the second in its own fiery collision; the view of the ship and **third Martian** is then lost in steam and smoke. Their definitive fates are not observed in that scene (`n0020`). The artilleryman's later assertion that the Martians have lost only one reflects **his limited knowledge**, not a corrected casualty total (`n0028`).
6. **Confinement and reversal:** During about **fifteen days** in the buried kitchen/scullery, the narrator sees Martian industry and feeding, quarrels with the curate, strikes him, and narrowly escapes a probing mechanical tentacle. On emerging he finds an alien-looking landscape overrun with **red weed**; the weed begins to decline from a presumed terrestrial disease (`n0023`–`n0027`).
7. **Last phase and aftermath:** The artilleryman's underground civilisation is revealed to be more oratory than labour. The narrator finds stationary Martians in London and reaches the **Primrose Hill** redoubt: they are dead, attributed to Earth microorganisms. In later reflection the explanation is called **strongly probable, not conclusively proved**. He undergoes a period of mental disturbance, is told Leatherhead was destroyed, returns to his house and unexpectedly reunites with his wife. The epilogue leaves future invasion and a possible Venus landing open (`n0028`–`n0031`).

## Recurring systems and concrete distinctions

- **Martians themselves:** Not humanoids. Mature creatures have enormous head-bodies (about four feet across), large eyes, beak-like mouth, sixteen fine tentacles in two groups, lungs and central nervous structures; weak terrestrial mobility; no digestive system as humans understand it. They take **fresh blood from living prey**, including humans, directly into their own circulation. Reproduction by **budding**, absence of sex and sleep, and purported freedom from disease are presented in the narrator's scientific retrospective (`n0007`, `n0023`–`n0024`). Mars-based bipedal **food animals** found in cylinders are **not Martians** (`n0023`).
- **Different machines:** The towering three-legged **fighting-machine** carries the operator, Heat-Ray and sometimes a carrier for captives (`n0013`–`n0015`, `n0022`). The agile, many-armed **handling-machine** works on materials and can probe the house (`n0023`–`n0025`). Also distinguish a digging/excavating mechanism, material-processing equipment that makes aluminium from clay, and an experimental **flying-machine** at Primrose Hill (`n0023`–`n0024`, `n0028`–`n0029`). The narrator stresses their supple, nearly organic articulation and the **absence of wheels**, contrary to anachronistic mechanical imagery (`n0023`).
- **Heat-Ray:** An effectively invisible directed beam of destructive heat; solid materials burn/melt and struck water erupts as steam. A parabolic-mirror account is **a theory, not verified mechanism**. Green smoke, light and sparks seen around equipment are not themselves the same as the invisible beam (`n0008`–`n0009`, `n0031`).
- **Black Smoke:** Not ordinary fire smoke. A canister releases a dense poisonous vapour that accumulates in hollows, can leave upper storeys relatively safer, reacts with water and eventually settles as **black dust/powder**. Martians also disperse it by **steam jets**. Its chemical composition remains unsettled (`n0018`, `n0022`, `n0031`). Do not confuse the poisoning with heat damage or the dark soot of conventional fires.
- **Red weed / red creeper:** Extraterrestrial growth spreads spectacularly after the Martian landing, particularly through **flowing water**, clogs rivers and causes flooding, then decays, apparently under the influence of local bacteria (`n0023`, `n0026`–`n0030`). The text also names a **“red creeper,”** once described as shorter-lived; do not silently assume that every reference denotes the same plant or that all colour terms refer to one botanical structure (`n0023`, `n0027`–`n0028`).
- **Sounds:** The metallic machines produce hoots and **“Aloo! Aloo!”** (`n0013`); a late stationary Martian emits the unending, mournful **“Ulla, ulla…”** (`n0029`). The narrator's retrospective **telepathy hypothesis** contests others' assumption that hooting is Martian conversation; he claims the hoot precedes feeding, but it remains an inference (`n0023`). Do not interpret the sound strings as confirmed words or translate them into invented dialogue.
- **Nineteenth-century context:** Heliographs, telegraph wires, special newspaper editions, horse artillery, hussars, Maxim guns, steam railways, horse-drawn cabs, bicycles, early motor cars and naval ironclads coexist. The **torpedo ram _Thunder Child_** is a distinct historical-style *type of warship*, not a modern missile boat or aircraft (`n0011`–`n0020`).

## Voice, motifs and ethical tensions

The texture alternates **measured speculative-scientific exposition**, precise topographical reportage and quoted dispatches, vivid physical terror, socially distinctive dialogue and abrupt psychological confession. The narrator can describe whole populations with the cool eye of a naturalist and then break into personal panic. He repeatedly addresses a reader presumed to live after the catastrophe (`n0004`, `n0009`, `n0011`, `n0020`, `n0031`). Preserve the switches instead of smoothing everything into heroic action prose.

A central reversal is **humanity becoming the animal or colonised subject**: microscopy, insects, ants, rabbits, dogs, the extinct dodo and dispossession recur. The opening invokes the destruction inflicted by European colonists on Indigenous Tasmanians and uses a nineteenth-century hierarchy of “inferior races” (`n0004`); the narrator later learns pity for the creatures humanity dominates (`n0027`–`n0028`). These passages are uncomfortable historically situated language, not terminology to endorse or unobtrusively sanitise. Class prejudice, military bravado, unreliable sensational journalism, religious collapse/repentance, survivalist eugenic fantasies and the narrator's own violence invite critical distance (`n0012`, `n0016`–`n0019`, `n0024`–`n0028`).

The catastrophe does **not** end in a straightforward military victory. Powerful human weapons occasionally wound or destroy machines, but the decisive reversal is attributed to microbes. The narrator's delight at recovery coexists with dislocation and recurring traumatic visions; his future remains insecure even with his wife alive (`n0029`–`n0031`). The epilogue imagines both a **human cosmic future** and renewed subjection. Keep the final balance unresolved.

## Ambiguities and open research questions

- **Disease explanation:** The main narration presents bacterial defeat as definite (`n0029`), but the epilogue acknowledges **Carver's hypothesis remains unproved** (`n0031`). Mark the difference between assertive storytelling and formal epistemic status; do not silently eliminate it.
- **Spectral particulars:** The early Black Smoke account refers to an unknown element yielding **four lines in the blue** (`n0018`), while the epilogue's analysis of its **black powder residue** says **three lines in the green** (`n0031`). They may concern different material states/observations, or be a source inconsistency; preserve the text and flag for later edition checking rather than harmonising it.
- **Martian communication:** Sound vs telepathy remains narrator-inferred; **Venus colonisation** is Lessing's suggestion, not a confirmed sequel; the circumstances and aims behind the cessation of the ten shots remain unknown (`n0004`, `n0023`, `n0031`).
- **Unseen fates:** The wife's escape from Leatherhead, the brother's later movements after leaving by sea, George Elphinstone's fate, and the naval encounter's obscured third Martian are not supplied in full (`n0020`, `n0030`). Maintain narrative gaps.
- **Human culpability:** The curate's actual moment of death occurs outside view and the narrator evaluates his own blow defensively; the artilleryman's harsh programme is undercut by his behaviour, not confirmed as a feasible salvation (`n0025`, `n0028`). Avoid certainties of motive or culpability beyond the words on the page.
- **Textual provenance:** Source notes cite an 1898 Heinemann first-edition record but **do not demonstrate that the Gutenberg transcription is copied from that edition**. The imported structural segmentation has not received independent human review. For contested spelling, punctuation, scientific discrepancies and attribution, compare an authenticated exemplar before making editorial corrections.

# The War of the Worlds — Japanese translation guide (`ja`)

**Working status:** All Japanese forms below are **provisional editorial suggestions, not approved translation decisions**. The supplied project notes establish the English work's *two-book, 17+10-chapter structure*, its front matter and its imported status; they establish **no published or human-approved Japanese translation or terminology policy**. Check existing Japanese editions and project preferences before freezing spelling, titles or voices. Source node IDs refer to the supplied structured work.

## Translation brief and register

Aim for **lucid, literary Japanese with an educated, retrospective first-person voice**, capable of moving from Edwardian-style essay and precise reportage into visceral terror. Prefer **「私」** as the narrator's consistent first-person self-reference in exposition. A restrained **だ／である** narrative register is a plausible starting point, but vary sentence rhythm, degree of formality and spoken pronouns according to situation. Do not mechanically reproduce every long English period as one sprawling Japanese sentence; preserve the **logic, suspense, repetitions and sudden perspective changes**. Avoid both excessive pseudo-Meiji archaism and casually contemporary SF jargon (`n0004`, `n0013`, `n0023`, `n0029`–`n0031`).

The narrator is *not* an omniscient hero. Distinguish **what he witnessed**, **what he was told**, **what he learned after the war**, **what he now believes**, and **what he admits remains open**. Japanese expressions such as **「らしい」「という」「後に知った」「おそらく」「断定はできない」** can preserve English hedging when warranted; avoid adding them to facts the source presents as direct observations. Conversely, do not turn speculations into plain declaratives. Keep the brother's separate itinerary in **third-person report**, rather than slipping into his first-person narration (`n0017`, `n0019`–`n0020`).

## Technology, biology and recurrent imagery

The following is a **contextual concordance**, not an enforced one-to-one dictionary.

| Original expression | Provisional Japanese base | Usage and exceptions |
|---|---|---|
| **cylinder / projectile / shot** | **円筒／飛来体・砲弾** | The interplanetary vehicle is a hot, screw-topped *cylinder*, not initially an identified spacecraft. In artillery/astronomy narration *shot* may be **砲弾**; when its nature is not yet known use **物体／飛来体**. Retain the gradually revealed artificial nature (`n0004`–`n0007`). |
| **the Thing** (often capitalised) | **その物体／それ／あの得体の知れないもの** | Use local suspense and focalisation. A single rigid noun or premature **宇宙船** would flatten the discovery (`n0004`–`n0007`). |
| **fighting-machine** | **戦闘機械** | If silhouette/action matters, **三脚歩行機械** or **三脚の巨機**. Avoid bare **戦闘機**, which now primarily means an aircraft. The mechanism contains a living Martian (`n0013`–`n0015`, `n0023`). |
| **tripod** | **三脚式の歩行機械／三本脚の巨体** | Literal **三脚** alone can imply a static stand. Do not confuse machine legs with Martian anatomy (`n0013`, `n0023`). |
| **handling-machine** | **作業機械／多腕作業機械** | A many-limbed manipulating machine, later used to search the ruins. **操作機械** might misleadingly imply a control panel. Keep it distinct from the fighting-machine (`n0023`–`n0025`). |
| **digging-machine / flying-machine** | **掘削機械／飛行機械** | Separate specialised devices; the latter is still an **experiment** before the Martians die, not a deployed air fleet (`n0023`, `n0028`–`n0029`). |
| **Heat-Ray** | **熱線** | Capitalised named weapon: consistent **熱線**; **熱線発生装置** for its generator. The destructive beam is invisible, despite accompanying light and smoke. Do **not** introduce **レーザー** or assume a proven mirror mechanism (`n0008`–`n0009`, `n0031`). |
| **Black Smoke** | **黒い毒煙** (or recurring shorter **黒煙**) | The weapon is a **heavy lethal vapour**, deliberately released from canisters. In context 「毒性の黒い蒸気」「黒い煙」 can read more naturally than repeating a formula. **Not** ordinary smoke from burning buildings; distinguish the **黒い粉／粉末** remaining after deposition (`n0018`, `n0022`, `n0031`). |
| **red weed** | **赤い草／赤い異星植物** | No single Japanese plant category fits every appearance: when it creeps up walls **赤い蔓草**, on water **赤い植物の葉状体** may fit. First mention can retain a naming formula (e.g., **「赤い草」と呼ばれる植物**). Avoid automatically **藻** or **雑草** in contexts of giant fronds and flooding (`n0023`, `n0026`–`n0030`). |
| **red creeper** | **赤い蔓草／赤い這い植物** | **Keep the original term distinction visible** until the botanical relationship is established; the text itself describes this as a transitory growth and elsewhere uses it around trees (`n0023`, `n0027`–`n0028`). |
| **hood / cowl / head of the machine** | **頭部の覆い／覆い付きの操縦部** | It encloses a Martian operator; do not confuse the **metallic hood** with the Martian's actual fleshy head (`n0014`–`n0015`, `n0023`). |
| **carrier / cage / basket** | **収容籠／金属製の籠** | Where humans are seized, the rear carrier is a terrifying practical device, not the vehicle's main body (`n0022`, `n0024`). |
| **tentacles** | **触手** | Used for Martian bodily appendages and flexible mechanical arms; when clarity requires, say **機械の触手／金属の腕** as appropriate (`n0007`, `n0013`, `n0023`). |
| **hands** (Martian tentacle groups) | **「手」** | Professor Howes's name for the two groups of eight fine tentacles; keep quotation/technical context, not ordinary human hands (`n0023`). |
| **hoot / “Aloo!” / “Ulla, ulla…”** | **鳴き声・唸り声／「アロー！」／「ウーラ、ウーラ……」** | The sound spellings are *approximate Japanese phonetic proposals only*. Once chosen, keep their sonic identity. The last wail is eerie and repetitive, **not** a translated sentence; avoid inventing Martian linguistic meanings (`n0013`, `n0023`, `n0029`). |
| **torpedo ram / ironclad** | **水雷衝角艦／装甲艦** | Period naval terminology for *Thunder Child* and surrounding warships. Do not recast it as a contemporary destroyer or submarine (`n0020`). |
| **heliograph / hussars / sappers / Maxims** | **日光反射通信器／軽騎兵／工兵／マキシム機関銃** | Establish a compact period vocabulary and keep it intelligible in action sequences (`n0011`–`n0018`). |

The **Martian head-body, lungs, brain, sixteen tentacles, blood-injection feeding, absence of digestion, budding reproduction and lack of sleep** are presented in a retrospective quasi-scientific idiom; let the passages sound informed **without asserting that these are modern biological facts** (`n0023`). Repeated words such as **“injected,” “veins,” “recipient canal,” “bacteria,” “putrefactive,”** and **“natural selection”** call for sober precise Japanese (**注入、血管、受け入れる管、細菌、腐敗、自然選択**) rather than theatrical monster-film terms. The narrator's claim that Martians communicate by **thought without a physical medium** is **his conviction**, not a discovered universal law (`n0023`).

## Narrator, dialogue and embedded registers

- **Essayist / investigator:** articulate, exact, willing to qualify his knowledge. Keep contrasts such as microscopic life vs human empire, and the repeated shifts **“then I thought” / “we now know” / “afterwards I learned.”** For the opening's long comparison, the clauses may be broken into two or three Japanese sentences as long as the ironic symmetry survives (`n0004`, `n0010`, `n0023`, `n0031`).
- **Inner crisis:** plain, compressed cries and physical details often interrupt elaborate sentences. Avoid melodramatic embellishment. His dissociation, shame, guilt and trauma should not be rendered as a uniformly stoic or triumphalist narration (`n0010`, `n0013`–`n0014`, `n0025`, `n0028`–`n0031`).
- **Artilleryman:** slang, dropped initial *h*, *ain't*, blunt class judgments and self-satisfied rhetoric. Prefer **colloquial, clipped Japanese** (e.g. 「もう負けだ」「生き延びるんだ」), perhaps a touch of rough masculine phrasing, but **do not invent a Japanese regional dialect** or make him sound inarticulate: he can reason persuasively at length (`n0012`, `n0014`–`n0015`, `n0028`). The later irony depends on the same fluent voice coexisting with laziness.
- **Curate:** initially shocked, later increasingly compulsive, Biblical and prophetic: repetitions, cries of **woe**, references to Sodom and Gomorrah, the day of the Lord and repentance. Use **聖書調の韻律** where the source quotes scripture; verify quotations against any chosen Japanese Bible version before claiming canonical wording. The narrator's rebuke **“He is not an insurance agent”** is deliberate dry irreverence and should remain sharp (`n0016`, `n0025`).
- **Mrs. / Miss Elphinstone:** Mrs. Elphinstone is anxious and repeatedly invokes **George**; the younger woman's decisiveness is shown in action more than ornate speech. Do not automatically assign genteel, old-fashioned feminine endings such as **「〜ですわ」** to every line; distinguish their temperament and roles instead (`n0019`–`n0020`).
- **Crowds and minor speakers:** paper-sellers, soldiers and workers supply short dialect-marked utterances, newspaper headlines and rumor. Natural colloquial contrasts suffice; do not turn nineteenth-century London class and accent variation into a collection of unrelated Japanese dialect caricatures (`n0007`, `n0012`, `n0017`, `n0019`).
- **Newspapers and military reports:** headings are often sensational or misleading. Give them abrupt display formatting where appropriate, distinct from the narrator's own claims. Retain titles such as *The Times*, *Daily Telegraph*, *Daily Chronicle* and *Daily Mail* as period markers, adding Japanese glosses only where useful (`n0004`, `n0006`, `n0017`, `n0030`).

## Editorial watchpoints for Japanese continuity

1. **Retrospective science is not a corrected textbook.** Preserve period terms and limits of certainty, including the speculative parabolic Heat-Ray mirror, Martian thought exchange, possible Venus landing and alleged microbe-free Mars. In `n0029`, the narrator declares bacteria the destroyers; in `n0031` he explicitly says Carver's explanation is *not a proven conclusion*. A Japanese rendering must retain that change in epistemic status.
2. **A source-level spectral discrepancy needs a note, not a hidden correction:** **four blue spectral lines** for the unknown element in `n0018` versus **three green lines** in the black-powder analysis of `n0031`. Both are in the supplied text. Preserve both unless independent edition review establishes an authorized emendation.
3. **Do not prematurely resolve unresolved fates.** The wife ultimately lives despite a report of Leatherhead's destruction (`n0030`); the brother's life after embarkation and George Elphinstone's fate are not specified (`n0020`). The curate is struck with the **blunt** end of the chopper, then taken away, not depicted being stabbed (`n0025`). The third Martian by the naval battle is obscured (`n0020`).
4. **Historical dehumanising language should remain attributable.** The opening's **“inferior races”** is a racist nineteenth-century hierarchy introduced as part of the narrator's argument about human colonial extermination (`n0004`). A historically faithful **「劣等人種」** in context, potentially supported by an editorial note, preserves the disturbing wording more honestly than either endorsing it in neutral narration or disguising the racial hierarchy. Similarly preserve the artilleryman's harsh distinction between “fit” survivors and disposable “weaklings” as **his own speech**, not an editorial recommendation (`n0028`).
5. **Metaphors form a network.** Tiny creatures under the microscope, ants crushed by people, the dodo, a hunted rabbit, sheep, the colonised and the Martians' “eatable ants” all reverse humanity's presumed dominion (`n0004`, `n0010`, `n0018`, `n0027`–`n0028`). Preserve the exact animal chosen in each place: reusing one generic **「虫けら」** everywhere would flatten the motif.
6. **Distinguish belief, fear and irony.** The narrator's confidence in military defeat of the invaders, the curate's eschatology and the artilleryman's underground utopia are repeatedly exposed as partial or self-serving. Do not remove the narrator's bitter humour or self-implication for the sake of a unified heroic voice (`n0010`, `n0016`, `n0025`, `n0028`).
7. **Keep typography/measurement policy stable but reviewable.** Japanese dialogue can use **「　」**, interior citations **『　』**, and em dashes/ellipses as needed. Preserve meaningful headline breaks, the unfinished prophecy **“In about two hundred years …”** (`n0030`), capitalisation of named weapons through consistent terminology, and the epigraph's **Kepler — quoted in *The Anatomy of Melancholy*** attribution (`n0001`). Retain imperial distances, pounds sterling and period military designations initially; if editorial policy later adopts conversions or modernised orthography, apply it systematically rather than silently.
